sources.locator: Learn Java; accessed 2026-07; Exceptions and Java I/O learning paths; atomic topic: Paths, files and text I/O
sources.claim: Modern Java file code uses Path and Files with an explicit charset, bounded data handling, and deliberate policies for absence, replacement, partial writes, and path resolution.

canonicalExplanation.summary: Modern Java file code uses **`Path`** (where a file is) and **`Files`** (what to do with it). Always pass an explicit **charset**, usually `StandardCharsets.UTF_8`, so text reads the same on every machine. A **relative path** is resolved against the **current working directory** of the running program, not the folder your source file lives in, so resolve paths from configuration or a known base. Decide your **policies** up front: what happens if the file is **missing** (NoSuchFileException), if the content is **malformed**, and whether a write may **replace** an existing file. Writing to a temp file and **moving** it into place avoids half-written files.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner's program reads `settings.txt` fine from the IDE but fails from the terminal: the relative path pointed somewhere else. On a colleague's machine, accented names come out garbled because no charset was given. And a missing file and a broken file both produce the same vague "could not load". A settings reader resolves a Path from configuration, reads UTF-8 text, validates every field, and distinguishes a missing file from malformed content. In this lesson you'll implement tested file persistence using modern path and file APIs.

examples.title: A settings reader that tells missing from broken
examples.situation: A settings reader resolves a Path from configuration, reads UTF-8 text, validates every field, and distinguishes a missing file from malformed content.
walkthrough: **Resolves a Path from configuration:** dir.resolve("settings.txt") builds it from a known base.
**Reads UTF-8 text, validates every field:** readAllLines uses UTF_8 and the port is range-checked.
**Distinguishes a missing file from malformed content:** NoSuchFileException versus IllegalStateException, so we handle each differently.
examples.result: Users get a clear message for each kind of problem.

examples.title: It works in my IDE
examples.situation: A program reading Path.of("data.csv") works in the IDE but fails from the terminal with NoSuchFileException.
walkthrough: The IDE and terminal had different working directories.
Print toAbsolutePath() to see the resolved location.
Take the base directory from configuration or an argument.
examples.result: The program finds its file from any directory.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: A relative filename always refers to the source-file directory, and Java text methods automatically choose the intended encoding.
misconceptions.correction: Relative paths resolve against the working directory, and omitting a charset can use a platform default. Resolve from a known base and pass UTF-8.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "It works in my IDE", why did the terminal run fail?

analogy.example: A relative path is like **directions saying "second door on the left"**: correct only if you start in the right hallway (the working directory). A charset is **the language a letter is written in**: if the reader guesses the wrong language, the words come out as nonsense.
usefulFor: remembering directions depend on the starting hallway
limitations: An absolute path is a full street address.
Temp-then-move is sealing the envelope before posting.
